summary: Ocean food webs for ages 7–9: multiple interconnected food chains where energy flows from phytoplankton (producers) through zooplankton, small fish, squid, seals and sharks. The core moves are seeing that most animals eat and are eaten by MORE THAN ONE thing (so a chain becomes a branching web), tracing energy along multiple paths, and reasoning about disturbance — removing one species and following the likely knock-on effects (a cascade) along several paths, both up to predators and down to prey. Outcomes are kept qualitative ('may increase/decline') rather than guaranteed.
misconceptions: 'A web is just a longer chain' — missing that the defining feature is multiple, branching feeding links.
Arrow reversal — reading arrows as 'eats' rather than 'energy flows to / is eaten by', more error-prone in a dense web.
'Removing a predator only helps' — not anticipating cascades (prey booms, overgrazes, other species crash).
'Only the directly-connected animal is affected' — not tracing effects along multiple/indirect paths.
'Top predators are most important; tiny plankton don't matter' — undervaluing producers at the web's base.

activities.title: Overlay chains to build a branching web, then pull one thread
steps: Start with two or three ocean food chains the child already knows (e.g. phytoplankton→zooplankton→small fish→squid→seals→sharks) and find the species they share.

Draw or drag 'energy flows to / is eaten by' arrows to join the chains where they share a species, so a single line becomes a branching WEB — notice that many animals now feed on, or are fed on by, more than one other species (though not every one: in this web sharks are not eaten by anything shown, and zooplankton eat only phytoplankton).
Check each arrow points from the eaten to the eater (energy flows to the eater); fix any reversed arrows.

Remove or crash one species (e.g. overfish the small fish) and trace the likely effects out loud along every connected arrow: predators that ate it (squid and seals) lose that food source and may decline; prey it used to eat (zooplankton) may increase; follow the ripple to indirectly connected species too (e.g. sharks that ate the squid and seals), which may also be affected.
Run two or three different removals and compare how far and in which directions each cascade may spread.
activities.insight: A food web is many food chains linked together: because most animals have multiple feeding links, removing one species can spread change along many paths at once, unlike a single straight chain where each animal has at most one link above and one below.

activities.title: Read a web: tap a species to see all its links
steps: On a pre-drawn ocean web, select a species and identify every arrow in and out of it — list all its predators and all its prey.
Count how many feeding links the species has to show it is part of a branching web, not a single chain.
For one species, state the first-order effects if it vanished (which neighbours directly lose food or lose a predator).
Tag each species as producer or consumer and note that energy flows upward from the plankton base and thins at each level as it rises (kept light at this age).
activities.insight: A web's defining feature is that species have multiple feeding links; you can read branching structure directly even before reasoning about cascades.

activities.title: Check understanding: web vs chain, trace a path, predict a removal
steps: Decide whether a given diagram is a web or a single chain and justify using the branching links.
Select and trace at least two different energy paths from the plankton base up to a top predator.
Given a removal scenario (e.g. almost all of one kind of small fish is fished out), predict the likely knock-on effects along more than one path and explain them.
activities.insight: Understanding is shown by distinguishing a branching web from a chain, tracing multiple energy paths, and predicting the likely cascading effects of a removal in both directions.

activities.title: Debate a fishing decision as a marine ecologist (supplementary)
steps: Take on an ecologist role responding to 'what happens if we fish out the sardines (small fish)?'
Predict the cascade out loud, naming animals that lose food, animals whose prey may increase, and any indirectly affected species.

Answer probing follow-ups: 'the small fish ate zooplankton — with the small fish gone, what happens to the zooplankton and why?'; 'why does damage spread further in a web than in a single chain?'; 'would a predator with three prey be hit as hard as one that ate only the lost prey?'
activities.insight: Articulating a predicted cascade in words rehearses multi-path reasoning and can surface whether the child can contrast web with chain.

checkQuestion: In an ocean food web, fishing boats catch almost all of one kind of small fish that many animals rely on. A child says: 'That only matters for those small fish — nothing else is really affected.' Do you agree? Trace what happens to the OTHER animals in the web, and tell me how a food web is different from a single food chain.
checkAnswer: Disagree — removing the small fish ripples through the whole web. Animals that ate the small fish (bigger fish, seabirds, seals) lose food and decline; the creatures the small fish used to eat (zooplankton) may increase; and predators higher up are affected too. A food WEB is many food chains linked together — most animals eat, and are eaten by, several others — so a change in one place spreads along many paths, unlike a single straight chain where each animal has just one link above and below.
